rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds while eluting strongly retained compounds. The retention window and limiting resolutions will guide gradient trimming and subsequent slope and temperature tests.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the crowded middle peaks respond to reduced slope. The initial last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution while likely keeping all peaks within 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient improved the limiting pair substantially, leaving only R=1.20 to address. Increase temperature by 5 °C to test selectivity changes while preserving the successful slope and gaining retention-time headroom.

The limiting pair converged sharply at 45 °C; testing 55 °C may carry it through an elution-order reversal into adequate separation. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature selectivity while shortening retention.

The temperature results suggest the limiting pair has reversed order, so a modestly steeper gradient may now increase its separation. Shorten tG to 12 minutes to test that prediction and reduce the last-peak time while retaining margin in the other pairs.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a slightly shallower gradient to seek a more balanced resolution margin between the two closest pairs. This small adjustment should keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Trim the gradient window while preserving injection 5’s slope and temperature to seek a shorter fully resolved method at the maximum CRF. The new starting fraction remains below the estimated first-peak elution fraction, and the endpoint remains above the last-peak elution fraction.

Reduce the slope to recover separation in the newly limiting pair while retaining the shorter programmed gradient. Earlier slope tests suggest the other close pair should retain enough resolution, with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 5’s starting composition, slope, and temperature while ending the gradient earlier, above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.57. This should reproduce its maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

With maximum CRF secured, test a faster method at higher temperature. The combined selectivity and slope changes may carry the crowded middle peaks through another order reversal, potentially restoring full resolution at a shorter retention time.

Shorten the gradient at fixed temperature to test whether the newly limiting pair separates further after its apparent order reversal. This explores a faster alternative while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as fallbacks.

The faster high-temperature gradients introduced additional unresolved pairs, so explore the low-temperature selectivity regime using the original scouting gradient. This tests a substantially different separation pattern while likely keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Return to the promising 40 °C selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve its limiting pair. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset some added retention time, potentially achieving full resolution below 10 minutes in an alternative temperature regime.

Reduce the slope from 0.057 to 0.050 organic fraction per minute to improve the remaining R=1.42 pair. Raise the starting fraction to offset the slower gradient and target complete resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 °C to separate the limiting middle pair on the opposite side of its apparent crossover. This may provide larger resolution margins than the existing maximum-score methods while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 14’s slope and temperature while shifting the gradient window upward to shorten retention. This tests whether its full resolution can be maintained with a faster last peak; the early pair still has substantial separation margin.

Reduce the slope slightly to recover the limiting pair’s resolution after the starting-composition increase. The current last peak at 8.59 minutes leaves time for this adjustment while targeting full resolution below 10 minutes.

Seek greater resolution margins around the successful 55 °C methods by combining a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient. This should spread the middle cluster while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and the earliest peaks retained.
Make the gradient slightly shallower to lift the remaining R=1.41 pair above 1.5. The other close pair has useful margin at R=1.74, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Use a slope slightly shallower than injection 8 to improve its R=1.55 limiting pair while aiming to preserve the other close pair above 1.5. This targets a maximum-score method with better resolution margins than injection 5 and shorter retention than injection 19.

Explore a faster high-temperature alternative by raising the starting organic fraction to shift the selectivity of the unresolved middle pair seen in injection 10. The slightly shallower slope may help preserve separation elsewhere in that cluster.

Raise the starting fraction another step to test further separation of the limiting middle pair, while reducing the slope to protect its neighboring pair. Monitor the earliest pair closely because its retention and separation may become limiting.

Return to the fully resolved region near injection 19 and increase the slope slightly to shorten retention while preserving its resolution margins. This targets another maximum-score method rather than further compressing the poorly resolved 60 °C separations.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 8 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at this starting composition. The limiting pair may approach R=1.5, while the last peak should move closer to the shortest established maximum-score method.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 20 to seek another fully resolved method with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes. The theoretical maximum CRF is already secured; this final run tests the resolution margin around that successful region.
